plan.contextChunk: This figure stacks two ray-tracing constructions, panel (a) for a concave mirror and panel (b) for a convex mirror, each drawn in cross section with the mirror as a pale curved arc on the right. In (a) a red upward arrow at the far left is labeled Object, its base P resting on the horizontal optical axis and its tip Q above; the axis also carries the points C, P prime, F, and the vertex V. Four color-coded rays numbered 1 through 4 leave Q: ray 1 in blue runs parallel to the axis and reflects back through F, ray 2 in red arrives along a line through F and leaves parallel to the axis, ray 3 in purple heads toward C and returns along itself with a small right-angle square at the mirror, and ray 4 in green strikes V and reflects symmetrically across the axis. All four cross at Q prime, the tip of a short red downward arrow labeled Image whose base P prime lies between C and F, and a small drawn eye at the lower left looks toward the mirror. Panel (b) repeats the construction on a convex mirror whose focal point F and center of curvature C lie behind the arc: the reflected rays spread apart, and their dashed backward extensions meet at Q prime, tip of a smaller upright red arrow labeled Image standing behind the mirror between V and F. Pairing the panels contrasts rays that genuinely converge with an image sitting only where extensions cross.

interactionPlan.concept: The image formed by a spherical mirror is located exactly where the principal rays (or their backward extensions) intersect, so a concave mirror can produce a real inverted image when rays truly converge or a virtual upright image when the object is inside the focal point, while a convex mirror always yields a virtual upright image because its reflected rays only ever diverge.
elements: horizontal optical axis line
spherical mirror drawn as a pale blue curved arc on the right (concave opening left in panel a, convex bulging left in panel b)
vertex point V where the arc meets the axis, labeled V
focal point F on the axis, labeled F (in front of mirror for concave, behind for convex)
center of curvature C on the axis, labeled C (in front for concave, behind for convex)
red upward object arrow with base P on the axis and tip Q, labeled Object
red image arrow with base P' on the axis and tip Q', labeled Image (downward/inverted for concave real case, upward/upright for virtual cases)
ray 1 (blue): from Q parallel to axis to mirror, reflected through F
ray 2 (red): from Q through F to mirror, reflected parallel to axis
ray 3 (purple): from Q toward C to mirror, reflected back on itself, with a small right-angle square at the mirror
ray 4 (green): from Q to vertex V, reflected symmetrically across the axis
number labels 1, 2, 3, 4 beside each ray
dashed backward extensions of the reflected rays meeting at Q' behind the mirror (convex case and concave virtual case)
small drawn eye icon at lower left looking toward the mirror
panel captions (a) and (b)

interactions.label: Mirror type
interactions.teaches: Switching mirror type flips where F and C sit and whether the reflected rays genuinely converge in front of the mirror (real image, concave) or spread apart so that only their dashed backward extensions meet behind it (virtual image, convex)

interactions.label: Object distance from mirror
interactions.teaches: Dragging the object along the axis moves, resizes, and flips the image: for a concave mirror the image is real and inverted when the object is outside F but becomes virtual, upright and magnified once the object crosses inside F; for a convex mirror the image stays virtual, upright and reduced at every position

Selecting one numbered ray isolates its single construction rule (1: parallel in, through F out; 2: through F in, parallel out; 3: through C, returns on itself; 4: hits V, reflects symmetrically), so each rule can be read off the busy crossing diagram one at a time

demo_steps.title: Concave mirror, object beyond C
demo_steps.narration: With the object far from a concave mirror, all four color-coded rays leave the tip Q and truly cross at Q' in front of the mirror, forming a real, inverted, reduced image between C and F.

demo_steps.title: Isolate one ray rule
demo_steps.narration: Click ray 1 (blue): it travels parallel to the axis and reflects straight through F. Clicking each numbered ray in turn reveals the one geometric rule behind it, building up the construction ray by ray.

demo_steps.title: Move the object inside F
demo_steps.narration: Drag the slider so the object sits between F and the mirror: the reflected rays now diverge, and only their dashed backward extensions meet behind the mirror, producing a virtual, upright, magnified image.

demo_steps.title: Convex mirror always virtual
demo_steps.narration: Toggle to the convex mirror: F and C move behind the arc, the reflected rays always spread apart, and their dashed extensions meet at an upright, reduced virtual image behind the mirror no matter where the object is placed.

interactionPlan.keyInsight: An image sits exactly where the principal rays intersect: when the rays themselves cross in front of the mirror the image is real and inverted, but when only their backward extensions cross behind the mirror the image is virtual and upright — concave mirrors can do both depending on object position, convex mirrors only the latter.
interactionPlan.reconstructionNotes: Lay out a single mirror panel at a time (per the toggle), not both stacked. Draw the optical axis horizontally with V at the mirror, then F and C along it (in front for concave, behind for convex). Object is a bold red upward arrow on the left labeled Object with base P and tip Q; image is a red arrow at P'/Q' labeled Image, drawn downward when real/inverted and upward when virtual/upright, with dashed segments for virtual images. Color the four rays consistently: ray 1 blue, ray 2 red, ray 3 purple, ray 4 green, each with its incident and reflected (or dashed extended) segment and a small number label; add a tiny right-angle square where ray 3 meets the mirror and a simple eye glyph at lower left. The mirror is a thin pale-blue arc. On slider change, recompute all four rays and the image arrow from the mirror equation so the convergence/divergence and the image's position, size and orientation update live; on ray click, dim the other three rays and brighten the selected one end to end.

authoredContext:
The figure shows a concave mirror and a convex mirror, each with an arrow-shaped object in front of it. These are the objects whose images we want to locate by ray tracing. To do so, we draw rays from point Q that is on the object but not on the optical axis. We choose to draw our ray from the tip of the object. Principal ray 1 goes from point Q and travels parallel to the optical axis. The reflection of this ray must pass through the focal point, as discussed above. Thus, for the concave mirror, the reflection of principal ray 1 goes through focal point F, as shown in part (b) of the figure. For the convex mirror, the backward extension of the reflection of principal ray 1 goes through the focal point (i.e., a virtual focus). Principal ray 2 travels first on the line going through the focal point and then is reflected back along a line parallel to the optical axis. Principal ray 3 travels toward the center of curvature of the mirror, so it strikes the mirror at normal incidence and is reflected back along the line from which it came. Finally, principal ray 4 strikes the vertex of the mirror and is reflected symmetrically about the optical axis.

The four principal rays shown for both (a) a concave mirror and (b) a convex mirror. The image forms where the rays intersect (for real images) or where their backward extensions intersect (for virtual images).

Figure a shows the cross section of a concave mirror. An upward arrow, labeled object, with base P and tip Q is in front of the mirror. A line connects points P, C, F and V, which is on the mirror. A downward arrow with base P prime and tip Q prime is labeled image. It is smaller than the object. P prime lies on the optical axis between points C and F. Four incident rays, labeled 1 through 4 originate from point Q. All four reflected rays intersect at point Q prime. Figure b shows the cross section of a convex mirror. An upward arrow, labeled object with base P and tip Q is in front of the mirror. A line from point P passes through point V on the mirror and point F behind the mirror before connecting to point C. A smaller, upward arrow, labeled image, with base P prime and tip Q prime is shown behind the mirror. P prime lies on the optical axis between points V and F. Four incident rays originate from point Q. The reflected rays are extended at the back with dotted lines and all seem to originate from point Q prime.

The four principal rays intersect at point Q′, which is where the image of point Q is located. To locate point Q′, drawing any two of these principal rays would suffice. We are thus free to choose whichever of the principal rays we desire to locate the image. Drawing more than two principal rays is sometimes useful to verify that the ray tracing is correct.

Object is a bold red upward arrow on the left labeled Object with base P and tip Q; image is a red arrow at P'/Q' labeled Image, drawn downward when real/inverted and upward when virtual/upright, with dashed segments for virtual images. Color the four rays consistently: ray 1 blue, ray 2 red, ray 3 purple, ray 4 green, each with its incident and reflected (or dashed extended) segment and a small number label; add a tiny right-angle square where ray 3 meets the mirror and a simple eye glyph at lower left. The mirror is a thin pale-blue arc. On slider change, recompute all four rays and the image arrow from the mirror equation so the convergence/divergence and the image's position, size and orientation update live; on ray click, dim the other three rays and brighten the selected one end to end.
